content: National tuberculosis (TB) prevalence surveys are critical for understanding the burden of TB disease in populations, especially in settings where routine surveillance systems are insufficient. They also help assess trends in TB burden over time, evaluate progress toward global targets, and inform national estimates of TB incidence and mortality. The World Health Organization (WHO) has played a central role in guiding and supporting these surveys. Since 2007, numerous national TB prevalence surveys have been conducted, particularly in high-burden countries. These surveys have provided valuable insights into the distribution of TB cases by age and sex, healthcare-seeking behaviors, and the extent of underreporting or underdiagnosis of TB cases. Findings from these surveys have been instrumental in improving TB case detection, diagnostic methods, and treatment interventions. Historically, the recommended diagnostic approach for TB prevalence surveys included sputum smear microscopy and culture testing. Culture testing, considered the microbiological reference standard for diagnosing Mycobacterium tuberculosis, requires stringent laboratory conditions, skilled personnel, and specialized equipment. However, culture testing has posed significant challenges in surveys, including maintaining a cold chain during sample transportation, preventing cross-contamination, managing high laboratory workloads, and ensuring timely processing of samples. These challenges have often led to delays, high contamination rates, and difficulties in standardizing techniques across multiple laboratories. In recent years, molecular diagnostic tools such as the Xpert MTB/RIF and Xpert Ultra assays have been increasingly used in TB prevalence surveys. These assays offer several advantages, including rapid results, automated processes, and less stringent laboratory requirements compared to culture testing. However, they also have limitations, such as lower sensitivity and specificity compared to liquid culture, and a higher likelihood of false-positive results for active TB disease in prevalence survey settings. Despite these limitations, the use of Xpert assays has become more common, particularly in surveys conducted after 2015. To address the challenges and variability in diagnostic algorithms used in TB prevalence surveys, WHO has developed updated recommendations for future surveys. These recommendations, based on extensive experience and new evidence, propose two major diagnostic options: 1. Option 1: Xpert Ultra-based survey – This approach involves testing all survey participants who screen positive (based on chest X-ray findings or reported symptoms) using the Xpert Ultra assay, followed by culture confirmation for those with Xpert Ultra-positive results. This option is expected to be the preferred choice in most countries due to its efficiency and practicality. 2. Option 2: This option may be considered in specific settings where culture testing infrastructure is robust. The updated guidance aims to minimize unnecessary diversity and inconsistency in diagnostic approaches across countries while ensuring reliable and comparable data. These recommendations are part of WHO’s broader efforts to support countries in achieving the milestones and targets outlined in the End TB Strategy and the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). In summary, national TB prevalence surveys remain a vital tool for measuring and addressing the burden of TB disease. The adoption of updated diagnostic algorithms, informed by lessons learned and new evidence, will enhance the quality and impact of these surveys in the years to come.
